(p-493) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And near over them will be its shade, and its clusters will be lowered in readiness.﴾ ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups that were crystal-like.﴾ ﴿Crystal-like, made of silver, which they have determined in measure.﴾ ﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger.﴾ ﴿A spring therein named Salsabil.﴾ ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys made eternal. If you saw them, you would think them scattered pearls.﴾ ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion.﴾

The grammarians differed over the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying, Exalted is He: "wa-daniyatan" (﴿and near﴾). Al-Zajjaj and others said it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) conjoined to "muttaki'īn" (reclining). He also said it may be an ṣifa (adjective) of the Garden, so the meaning is: "and He rewarded them with a near Garden." The majority of readers recite "daniyatan," al-A'mash recites "wa-daniyan 'alayhim," Abu Ḥaywa recites "wa-daniyatun" with the nominative, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b recites "wa-dānin," which is singular and nominative in its grammatical position. The nearness of the shades is by the extension of their bounty, because a shading object, when it is distant, its shade becomes weak, especially of trees. And "tadhlīl" (lowering) is that the fruit ripens and hangs down and bends toward the ground. The lowering in the Garden is according to the will of its inhabitants. Qatada, Sufyan and Mujahid said: if the person is standing, he takes the fruit without difficulty; and if he is sitting, likewise; and if he is lying down, likewise. This is its lowering: distance does not keep the hand from it, nor does a thorn. From the same root is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"…like the well-lowered pipe of the water-channel"

And from it is the saying of the Ansari: "The palm trees have been lowered, so they are encircled by their fruit." And "quṭūf" is the plural of "qiṭf," which is a cluster of dates, grapes and the like.

"Ānniyah" is the plural of "inā'," and "kūb" is what has no handle or ear among the vessels. Its shape is well known in those lands, and it is what the common people call "qabb." His Almighty and Majestic saying:

﴿Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver, and their Lord will give them a pure drink to drink.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is a reward for you, and your striving has been appreciated.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an, sending it down progressively.﴾ ﴿So be patient for the decision of your Lord, and do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever.﴾ ﴿And mention the name of your Lord morning and evening.﴾ ﴿And during the night, prostrate to Him and glorify Him for a long part of the night.﴾

Nafi', Hamza, and Aban, on the authority of 'Asim, read "ʿāliyahum" (عَالِيَهُمْ) with a nominative (raf') ending, as a beginning of a sentence (mubtada'). This is the reading of al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ibn 'Abbas (with a variant transmission from him). The rest of the readers, and 'Asim, read "ʿāliyahum" with an accusative (naṣb) ending, as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the governing element in it is "laqqāhum" or "jazāhum". This is the reading of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, and the people of Makkah. Al-A'mash and Talha read "ʿāliyatuhum" (عَالِيَتُهُمْ), and it is likewise in the codex of 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud). Al-A'mash also read "ʿāliyatahum" (عَالِيَتَهُمْ) with an accusative ending, as a circumstantial clause. In both accusative readings it is also permissible that it be an adverb of place (ẓarf), since it carries the meaning of "above them" (fawqahum). 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, read "ʿalathum" (عَلَتْهُمْ) with a tā' as a past-tense verb. Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Sirin, and Abu Haywa read "ʿalayhim" (عَلَيْهِمْ) with a yā'.

"Sundus" (السُنْدُسُ) is the thin brocade and its finer part. It is said that "sundus" is green silk. "Istabraq" (الإسْتَبْرَقُ) and "dimaqs" (الدِمْقَسُ) are white, and "urjuwan" (الأُرْجُوانُ) is red. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "khuḍrin wa istabraqin" (خُضْرٍ وإسْتَبْرَقٍ) with a genitive (khafḍ) ending in both, and this is the reading of al-A'mash, Talha, and it is related from al-Hasan and Ibn 'Umar (with a variant transmission from them), on the basis that "khuḍran" is an attribute (na't) of "sundus". It is permissible to use a plural adjective for a collective noun (ism al-jins) when it is a singular noun, as they said: "The yellow dinar has ruined people, and the white dirham," but this is unsightly. The Arabs sometimes use a singular form for a collective noun that is plural, so they say: "He is a white pebble (ḥaṣan abyaḍ)." Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 76, verses 27–31:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿Indeed, these love the immediate life and leave behind them a heavy Day.﴾ ﴿We created them and strengthened their frame, and when We wish, We can replace their likes with a complete replacement.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way.﴾ ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy, while for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment.﴾

The indication by "these" (hā'ulā') is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and "the immediate life" (al-'ājila) is the worldly life, and their love for it is that they do not believe in anything other than it. ﴿And leave behind them﴾ means: in the time that comes after their death. Labid said:

Is it not that after me, if my death is delayed, there is the staff's obligation, upon which the fingers are bent?

Describing the Day as "heavy" is by way of attribution (nisba), meaning: possessing heaviness, in that the heaviness in it falls upon the disbelievers; so it is like "a sleeping night."

Then He enumerated the blessing upon His servants in their creation and bringing into existence, the perfection of their form and the firmness of their constitution. "Al-Asr" is the constitution, the harmony of the limbs and the joints. Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan and al-Rabi' said: "al-Asr" means the joints and the connecting parts. Some have said: al-Asr is strength, and from it is the poet's saying:

He saved him, on the morning of death, from me, [one] of strong build, who bit upon the bridle.

And another's saying:

From every swerving one, strong of build, smooth of leading, you think him proud.

Al-Tabari said: From it is the common saying: "Take him with his asr," meaning: take all of him.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The origin of this is in that which has binding and tying, like a bone and the like, and this is not peculiar to the common people; rather it is from the eloquent speech of the Arabs. Unless by "the common people" one means the majority of the Arabs. From the same root is "al-isar," which is the shackle with which the captive is bound.

Then He threatened with replacement, and there is gathered from the two statements the enumeration of the blessing and the warning of replacement, a proof against those who deny resurrection, meaning: from this bringing into existence and replacement, if He wills, is within His power; so how would resurrection be beyond Him?

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ may refer to this verse, or to the whole surah, or to the Sharia in its entirety. His saying: ﴿whoever wills﴾ is not by way of granting choice; rather it contains an indication of warning and urging to take the way. And "the way" here is not salvation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ is a negation of their power to originate and bring into existence meanings in their souls; and this is not contradicted by their existing acquisition and inclination toward disbelief. Abdullah read: "And you do not will except what Allah wills." Yahya ibn Wathhab read "tishā'ūn" with a kasra on the taa'. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Knowing, Wise﴾ means: He knows what should be made easy for His servant toward, and in that is a wisdom known to none but Him.

"The wrongdoers" is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: and He punishes the wrongdoers, for them He has prepared. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "wa-li-l-zālimīna a'adda lahum," with the lam repeated. The majority of the Seven read "wa-mā tashā'ūn" with the taa' as address; Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "yashā'ūn" with the yaa'. Ibn al-Zubayr, Aban ibn 'Uthman and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-l-zālimūn" with the raf'; Abu al-Fath said: this is on the improvisation of a resumed sentence.

Here ends the tafsir of Surat [al-Insan], and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

﴿Indeed, these love the immediate life and leave behind them a heavy Day.﴾ ﴿We created them and strengthened their frame, and when We wish, We can replace their likes with a complete replacement.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way.﴾ ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy, while for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment.﴾

The indication by "these" (hā'ulā') is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and "the immediate life" (al-'ājila) is the worldly life, and their love for it is that they do not believe in anything other than it. ﴿And leave behind them﴾ means: in the time that comes after their death. Labid said:

Is it not that after me, if my death is delayed, there is the staff's obligation, upon which the fingers are bent?

Describing the Day as "heavy" is by way of attribution (nisba), meaning: possessing heaviness, in that the heaviness in it falls upon the disbelievers; so it is like "a sleeping night."

Then He enumerated the blessing upon His servants in their creation and bringing into existence, the perfection of their form and the firmness of their constitution. "Al-Asr" is the constitution, the harmony of the limbs and the joints. Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan and al-Rabi' said: "al-Asr" means the joints and the connecting parts. Some have said: al-Asr is strength, and from it is the poet's saying:

He saved him, on the morning of death, from me, [one] of strong build, who bit upon the bridle.

And another's saying:

From every swerving one, strong of build, smooth of leading, you think him proud.

Al-Tabari said: From it is the common saying: "Take him with his asr," meaning: take all of him.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The origin of this is in that which has binding and tying, like a bone and the like, and this is not peculiar to the common people; rather it is from the eloquent speech of the Arabs. Unless by "the common people" one means the majority of the Arabs. From the same root is "al-isar," which is the shackle with which the captive is bound.

Then He threatened with replacement, and there is gathered from the two statements the enumeration of the blessing and the warning of replacement, a proof against those who deny resurrection, meaning: from this bringing into existence and replacement, if He wills, is within His power; so how would resurrection be beyond Him?

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ may refer to this verse, or to the whole surah, or to the Sharia in its entirety. His saying: ﴿whoever wills﴾ is not by way of granting choice; rather it contains an indication of warning and urging to take the way. And "the way" here is not salvation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ is a negation of their power to originate and bring into existence meanings in their souls; and this is not contradicted by their existing acquisition and inclination toward disbelief. Abdullah read: "And you do not will except what Allah wills." Yahya ibn Wathhab read "tishā'ūn" with a kasra on the taa'. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Knowing, Wise﴾ means: He knows what should be made easy for His servant toward, and in that is a wisdom known to none but Him.

"The wrongdoers" is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: and He punishes the wrongdoers, for them He has prepared. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "wa-li-l-zālimīna a'adda lahum," with the lam repeated. The majority of the Seven read "wa-mā tashā'ūn" with the taa' as address; Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "yashā'ūn" with the yaa'. Ibn al-Zubayr, Aban ibn 'Uthman and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-l-zālimūn" with the raf'; Abu al-Fath said: this is on the improvisation of a resumed sentence.

Here ends the tafsir of Surat [al-Insan], and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
